description: Assesses the appropriate hosting and compute model for the workload based on service type, traffic profile, team capability, and platform availability.

recommendation.rationale: Public-facing services with spiky or unpredictable traffic benefit from serverless compute which scales to zero and handles burst traffic without pre-provisioning. This reduces cost during quiet periods and eliminates capacity planning risk.

operationalBurden.staffingImplications: No dedicated infrastructure team required; developers manage function deployments
operationalBurden.ongoingMaintenance: Minimal infrastructure maintenance; focus on function code, dependency updates, and cold-start optimisation

costConsiderations.runningCosts: Pay-per-invocation model; cost scales linearly with usage; zero cost at zero traffic
costConsiderations.transitionCosts: Application refactoring to event-driven model; team upskilling on serverless patterns

recommendation.rationale: Public-facing services with steady or growing traffic are well-suited to containerised deployments. Containers provide consistent environments, efficient resource utilisation, and horizontal scaling without the cold-start penalties of serverless.

operationalBurden.staffingImplications: Requires team familiarity with container orchestration; managed services reduce but do not eliminate operational overhead
operationalBurden.ongoingMaintenance: Container image updates, security patching, scaling policy tuning, and cluster maintenance (if self-managed)

costConsiderations.runningCosts: Predictable monthly costs based on reserved capacity; auto-scaling adds variable component
costConsiderations.transitionCosts: Containerisation of existing application; CI/CD pipeline setup; team training

recommendation.rationale: Internal services with teams that have limited cloud experience benefit from PaaS offerings that abstract infrastructure complexity. This allows the team to focus on application logic while the platform handles scaling, patching, and availability.

operationalBurden.staffingImplications: Standard development team can manage; no specialist infrastructure skills required
operationalBurden.ongoingMaintenance: Application code updates and dependency management; platform handles OS patching and scaling

costConsiderations.runningCosts: Fixed monthly cost based on tier selection; predictable and easy to budget
costConsiderations.transitionCosts: Minimal; standard web applications deploy with little modification

recommendation.rationale: Batch processing workloads are ideal for serverless or managed compute services that provision resources on demand and release them when processing completes. This avoids paying for idle compute between batch runs.

operationalBurden.staffingImplications: Development team manages job definitions and scheduling; no infrastructure team needed
operationalBurden.ongoingMaintenance: Job definition updates, monitoring for failed runs, and periodic review of processing times

costConsiderations.runningCosts: Pay only for compute time during batch execution; zero cost between runs
costConsiderations.transitionCosts: Refactoring batch jobs to cloud-native patterns; setting up orchestration

recommendation.rationale: API services with steady traffic and high availability requirements benefit from containerised deployments with auto-scaling and health checks. Containers provide consistent performance without cold-start latency, which is critical for API SLAs.

operationalBurden.staffingImplications: Requires container expertise; managed services reduce operational load significantly
operationalBurden.ongoingMaintenance: Container image updates, API versioning management, performance tuning, and SLA monitoring

costConsiderations.runningCosts: Predictable costs based on minimum replica count; auto-scaling adds variable costs during peaks
costConsiderations.transitionCosts: Containerisation effort; API gateway configuration; monitoring setup

recommendation.rationale: Data platforms and integration layers with experienced teams benefit from managed Kubernetes or equivalent orchestration. This provides the flexibility to run diverse workloads (APIs, workers, schedulers) in a unified platform with sophisticated scaling and deployment strategies.

operationalBurden.staffingImplications: Requires dedicated platform engineering capability; at least one Kubernetes-experienced engineer
operationalBurden.ongoingMaintenance: Cluster upgrades, node pool management, security patching, RBAC management, and capacity planning

costConsiderations.runningCosts: Control plane costs plus node compute; can be significant for small workloads
costConsiderations.transitionCosts: Significant team upskilling; platform engineering investment; migration effort

recommendation.rationale: Without cloud platform access, the workload must be hosted on existing on-premises infrastructure or delivered via SaaS products. This limits scalability options but may align with existing organisational constraints and security postures.

operationalBurden.staffingImplications: Requires dedicated infrastructure team for hardware, networking, patching, and capacity management
operationalBurden.ongoingMaintenance: Hardware lifecycle management, OS patching, capacity planning, physical security, and disaster recovery testing

costConsiderations.runningCosts: Capital expenditure for hardware; ongoing costs for power, cooling, licensing, and staff
costConsiderations.transitionCosts: Hardware procurement lead times; data centre space; network connectivity

defaultRecommendation.rationale: When no specific conditions strongly favour an alternative, a managed container service provides a good balance of flexibility, scalability, and operational simplicity. It supports most workload types without requiring deep specialist knowledge.

operationalBurden.staffingImplications: Standard development team with basic cloud knowledge can manage
operationalBurden.ongoingMaintenance: Container image updates, scaling policy reviews, and cost monitoring

commonQuestions: What is the expected traffic pattern and peak load?
Does the team have experience with container orchestration?
Are there existing hosting contracts or commitments that constrain platform choice?
What is the acceptable cold-start latency for the service?
Is there a requirement to run in multiple availability zones?
What is the deployment frequency expectation?
evidenceNeeded: Traffic volume estimates and peak load projections
Team skills assessment for container and cloud technologies
Performance requirements including response time SLAs
artefactsToProduce: Compute sizing and scaling strategy document
Cost estimate for chosen hosting model
